pageData.title: The Study of History & the Rise of Civilizations
pageData.para1:
The Study of History & the Rise of Civilizations. History is the study of the human past through evidence. Historians do not simply memorize dates; they ask how we know what happened, and they test claims against sources. The raw material of history comes in several kinds. Written sources include inscriptions on stone and clay, letters, tax records, law codes, king lists, and chronicles. Material sources come from archaeology: buildings, tools, pottery, weapons, jewelry, and even seeds and bones that reveal what people grew and ate. Oral traditions, such as epics sung for generations before being written down, preserve memory but must be read with care, because they mix real events with legend. A careful historian compares sources against each other.

When an Assyrian king boasts that he destroyed a city, and archaeologists find a burned layer in that city's ruins dated to the right years, the two sources confirm each other. When sources disagree, historians ask who wrote each one, when, and why, because every author had a purpose. To organize the past, historians divide time into periods. Prehistory is the long span before writing; history in the strict sense begins when people start keeping written records, which happened first in Sumer and Egypt around 3200-3000 BC. Events are dated BC (Before Christ) or AD (Anno Domini), and modern scholars often use BCE and CE, which count the same years. Timelines let us see which societies existed at the same time: the pyramids of Giza were already ancient when Abraham lived, and Athens was building the Parthenon while Japan was still in its age of rice-farming villages.
pageData.para2:
A civilization is a complex way of organizing human life, and this course traces four of them: Egypt, Iraq (Mesopotamia), Greece, and Japan. Civilizations share common features, and understanding these features explains why they appeared where they did. The first requirement is a food surplus. When farming produces more grain than farmers themselves eat, some people are freed to become potters, priests, soldiers, scribes, and kings. This is why the earliest civilizations rose along great rivers: the Nile in Egypt, and the Tigris and Euphrates in Iraq, where floodwater made dry land fertile. The second feature is cities, dense settlements where specialization and trade could flourish. The third is government: leaders who organize labor, collect taxes, enforce laws, and lead armies. The fourth is writing, invented first to record grain deliveries and debts, then used for laws, letters, literature, and history itself.

The fifth is organized religion, which explained the world, justified rulers, and bound communities together through shared rituals and temples. Finally come monumental building and specialized art, from pyramids and ziggurats to temples and sculpture, which displayed a society's wealth and beliefs. Civilizations also interact. Mesopotamia and Egypt traded with each other through the Levant; Greece learned writing from the Phoenicians and mathematics from Egypt and Babylon; Japan deliberately imported writing, Buddhism, and government models from China and Korea. No civilization developed in isolation, and no civilization lasts forever: each unit of this course follows its society from rise, through achievement, to decline, and asks what later peoples learned from it. The course also asks why civilizations rise and decline, and the rivers are only the beginning of the answer.

Egypt was protected by deserts and sea, which let one kingdom endure for three thousand years; Iraq's open plain made it rich and invaded in turn by Sumerians, Akkadians, Babylonians, Assyrians, Persians, Greeks, Arabs, and Mongols, so that its history is a story of successive empires; Greece, cut into valleys and islands by mountains, never unified but produced fiercely independent city-states whose rivalry drove both war and creativity; Japan, an island chain protected by the sea yet close enough to learn from China, could choose when to open and when to close, a freedom Egypt and Iraq never had. Geography is not destiny, but it sets the terms on which peoples make their history.

The other great lesson is that civilizations decline from within as much as from without: empires fall when taxes crush the peasants, when elites fight for power, when armies become kingmakers, or when the center can no longer maintain the canals, roads, and trust on which everything rests. Students who learn to see these patterns in Sumer, Egypt, Greece, and Japan are learning to read their own world. Writing itself deserves a place among the marks of civilization, because it changed what humans can remember and therefore what they can build. Before writing, knowledge died with the elders; after it, laws, observations, stories, and accounts accumulated beyond any single memory, and societies could administer kingdoms too large for any king to see.

It is no accident that the first scripts, Sumerian cuneiform and Egyptian hieroglyphs, appeared within centuries of the first cities, or that the earliest texts are mostly lists of grain, labor, and goods: the state was writing's first customer. Only later did writing turn to literature, law, and history, the uses that let civilizations reflect on themselves. Students should also notice what civilization costs: monuments were raised by taxes and labor, cities bred disease and hierarchy, and the freedom of the scribe rested on the toil of the farmer. History honestly told includes both the pyramid and the hands that built it. That double vision, wonder at what humans achieved together and honesty about its price, is the habit this course tries to teach, because a civilization's story, like a student's, is measured not only by its glories but by what it learned.

pageData.title: The Old Kingdom of Egypt
pageData.para1:
The Old Kingdom of Egypt. Around 3100 BC, King Narmer of Upper Egypt united the Two Lands, the Nile Valley in the south and the Delta in the north, into a single kingdom, the first large territorial state in human history. After two dynasties of consolidation, the Old Kingdom proper began with the Third Dynasty around 2686 BC, and it is remembered above all as the age of the pyramids. King Djoser's architect Imhotep stacked six mastaba tombs into the Step Pyramid at Saqqara, the first monumental stone building in the world. In the Fourth Dynasty, Sneferu built three pyramids, experimenting with the bent and true forms, and his son Khufu raised the Great Pyramid at Giza: about 2.3 million stone blocks, aligned to the cardinal points with astonishing precision, the tallest human structure for more than 3,800 years.

Khafre and Menkaure added their own pyramids beside it, guarded by the Great Sphinx. These were not tombs built by slaves, as old films suggest, but national projects carried out by rotating crews of paid laborers, fed and housed in workers' towns, organized by a state that could count, store, and redistribute grain on a vast scale. Royal authority was supported by governors called nomarchs, who administered the provinces or nomes, and by a vizier who ran the bureaucracy. Over time, however, the crown's wealth drained into temple endowments and provincial families. The unusually long reign of Pepi II, perhaps over ninety years in the Sixth Dynasty, ended with an aging court and ambitious local rulers. Around 2181 BC central authority collapsed, provincial magnates fought for power, and famine struck as Nile floods failed.

Egypt fragmented into the First Intermediate Period, and the lesson was lasting: Egyptian unity depended on a strong center that could manage the river and the harvest. The unification itself is pictured on the Narmer Palette, where the king wears the crowns of both lands and smites his enemies, an image of kingship that Egyptians would repeat for three thousand years. The central government that emerged was the first true state: it assessed the land, levied the harvest, and mobilized tens of thousands for building, and its records in ink on papyrus and stone show an administration counting everything from cattle to work gangs. Pyramid building itself was economic policy as much as religion: in the flood season, when the fields lay under water, the state employed the farmers, fed them from its granaries, and bound the provinces to the crown through common work.

The standard of the age was order: texts boast that the king upheld ma'at against chaos, and the bureaucracy of scribes, with its titles, seals, and archives, made Egypt the most organized society of the ancient world. When that order broke down after Pepi II, the sages who wrote the lamentations of the First Intermediate Period remembered anarchy as the Nile's gift ungiven: the land spun like a potter's wheel, they said, and the poor became rich while the rich begged, an inversion of the sacred order that Egyptians felt in their bones as catastrophe.
pageData.para2:
Old Kingdom society was shaped by the Nile. The river flooded predictably each summer, depositing rich silt; farmers planted wheat and barley as the waters receded and harvested in spring. This dependable cycle created the surplus that fed pyramid builders and priests, and it explains why Egyptians saw the world as fundamentally ordered and good. At the top stood the pharaoh, not merely a king but a living god, the son of Ra and the earthly form of Horus, responsible for maintaining ma'at, the cosmic order of justice, balance, and truth. Below him came viziers, priests, and scribes, whose mastery of hieroglyphic and cursive hieratic writing gave them control of records and therefore of power. Most people were peasant farmers who paid taxes in grain and owed labor service to the state.

Religion permeated everything: Egyptians worshipped many gods, above all the sun god, and believed in an afterlife that the king's pyramid was built to secure. The Pyramid Texts inscribed in the later pyramids are the world's oldest religious writings, and the same beliefs drove mummification and the stocking of tombs with food, furniture, and servant statues. Art followed a strict canon: the human figure shown with head and legs in profile, eye and shoulders frontal, proportioned on a grid, built to last for eternity rather than to imitate a fleeting moment. Trade reached south to Nubia for gold, east to Punt for incense, and north to Byblos for Lebanese cedar. Mathematics served surveying and engineering, medicine produced some of the earliest written case studies, and a solar calendar of 365 days, divided into flood, planting, and harvest seasons, organized the year.

The Old Kingdom created the pattern of Egyptian civilization that later ages would look back to as their classical ideal.

pageData.title: The Middle Kingdom of Egypt
pageData.para1:
The Middle Kingdom of Egypt. After a century of division, Egypt was reunified around 2055 BC by Mentuhotep II of Thebes, who defeated his northern rivals and reopened the roads, mines, and trade routes that civil war had closed. His dynasty gave way to the Twelfth Dynasty, founded by Amenemhat I around 1985 BC, who moved the capital to the new planned city of Itjtawy near the Faiyum and, in a strikingly honest text called the Instruction of Amenemhat, warned his son to trust no one, having survived an assassination attempt. The Twelfth Dynasty ruled Egypt for nearly two centuries, one of the most stable and productive periods in its history.

Sesostris III broke the power of the old provincial nomarch families, reorganized the kingdom into three administrative districts, and pushed the southern frontier past the Second Cataract of the Nile into Nubia, where he built a chain of massive mud-brick fortresses such as Buhen and Semna to control the gold trade. His successors turned to the Faiyum depression west of the Nile, where Amenemhat III oversaw a huge land-reclamation project: dikes and canals regulated the lake, and new farmland expanded the kingdom's food supply. Middle Kingdom kings still built pyramids, but now of mud brick with stone casings, smaller and less enduring than those at Giza. After Amenemhat III, a series of short reigns weakened the dynasty, and the Thirteenth Dynasty rotated kings rapidly while central authority slipped away.

Around 1650 BC the Hyksos, a people of western Asian origin who had settled in the Delta and adopted Egyptian customs, seized power in the north, ruling from Avaris with superior military technology: the horse-drawn chariot, the composite bow, and bronze weapons. Egypt split again in the Second Intermediate Period, but the Hyksos occupation would teach Egyptians the new arts of war they needed to build an empire. The reunification was remembered as the work of a second founder, and the Theban kings governed consciously in the shadow of the pyramid age, reviving its styles while correcting its mistakes. Amenemhat I created a professional standing army and, to guard the approaches from Asia, built the Walls of the Ruler in the eastern Delta, the first of Egypt's frontier defenses.

The Nubian fortresses of Sesostris III were a military system complete with signal stations and supply depots, and his boundary stele at Semna forbade Nubians to pass except for trade, an early document of border control. The Faiyum project, with its great lake and canal network, added tens of thousands of acres and was remembered in the Greco-Roman age as the work of a king called Moeris. Egypt now projected power abroad as never before: expeditions reopened the Red Sea route to Punt, mining camps worked the copper and turquoise of Sinai, and Egyptian influence reached deep into Syria and Palestine, where rulers paid court to Thebes. The dynasty also managed succession carefully through co-regency, the old king crowning his heir in his lifetime so that power passed without civil war, a hard-won lesson from the chaos that had destroyed the Old Kingdom.
pageData.para2:
The Middle Kingdom is remembered as Egypt's classical age of literature. In Middle Egyptian, the dialect that schoolchildren would copy for a thousand years, writers produced works of real literary ambition. The Tale of Sinuhe follows a courtier who flees Egypt after a royal assassination, makes his fortune in Syria, and longs in old age to return and be buried at home, a meditation on exile and identity. The Eloquent Peasant dramatizes a wronged farmer whose beautiful speeches force officials to grant him justice, reflecting the period's emphasis on ma'at as a duty the powerful owe the weak. The Instruction of King Merikare advises a ruler to govern well because even kings are judged after death. This literature survives because scribal schools copied it for centuries, and it tells us that Middle Kingdom Egyptians were wrestling with questions of justice, loyalty, and mortality. Religion changed profoundly in this era.

Belief in the afterlife, once reserved for the king, was extended to ordinary officials and commoners. Osiris, god of the afterlife, became the hope of everyone, and guidance texts painted inside wooden coffins gave non-royal Egyptians what had once been reserved for kings. Society became somewhat more mobile; a capable scribe or soldier could rise, and Egyptians began to speak of self-made men. Craftsmanship reached extraordinary refinement: the gold jewelry of princesses like Sithathoryunet, with cloisonne inlay of colored stones, has never been surpassed. Block statues, squatting figures wrapped in cloaks, offered a new sculptural form for tombs and temples. Trade expeditions sailed to Punt for myrrh and incense and to Lebanon for cedar, while forts in Nubia secured gold, ivory, and ebony. The Middle Kingdom proved that Egypt could be reborn after collapse, a pattern of fragmentation and reunification that would repeat through its long history.

pageData.title: The New Kingdom of Egypt
pageData.para1:
The New Kingdom of Egypt. Around 1550 BC, Ahmose I of Thebes drove the Hyksos out of the Delta and pursued them into Canaan, founding the Eighteenth Dynasty and the era of empire. Determined never again to be ruled by foreigners, Egypt's warrior pharaohs pushed outward. Thutmose I campaigned as far as the Euphrates River in Syria. His daughter Hatshepsut then ruled as pharaoh in her own right for about twenty years, presenting herself in statuary with the king's kilt and false beard, building her terraced mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari, and sending a celebrated trading expedition to the land of Punt, whose ships returned loaded with incense trees, gold, and exotic animals.

Her stepson Thutmose III became Egypt's greatest conqueror: in seventeen campaigns he defeated a coalition of Canaanite kings at Megiddo around 1457 BC, crossed the Euphrates, and organized an empire stretching from Nubia deep into Syria, held together by garrisons, tribute, and the sons of vassal princes raised at the Egyptian court. Under Amenhotep III the empire enjoyed a golden age of wealth and diplomacy, its capital at Thebes glittering with temples. Then came the strangest episode in Egyptian history: Amenhotep IV, renaming himself Akhenaten, suppressed the old gods, closed their temples, and proclaimed one god, the sun disk Aten, building a new capital at Amarna. The experiment collapsed with his death; the boy king Tutankhamun restored the old religion and died young, his intact tomb the greatest archaeological find of the modern age.

In the Nineteenth Dynasty, Ramesses II fought the Hittite Empire at Kadesh around 1274 BC, a battle he claimed as a victory that was probably a draw, and later signed with the Hittites the world's oldest surviving peace treaty. His long reign left colossal monuments including Abu Simbel. Around 1175 BC Ramesses III repelled the Sea Peoples, but the effort exhausted the treasury, strikes hit the royal tomb builders, and the New Kingdom slowly dissolved. The empire was run as a system. In Nubia, a viceroy called the King's Son of Kush governed from fortified temple towns down to the Fourth Cataract, shipping gold north in quantities that made Egypt the richest state of the Bronze Age. In Asia, Egyptian strategy rested on the loyalty of Canaanite city-kings, bound by oaths, hostages, and gifts, and on the great fortress and granary cities that anchored the military roads.

Diplomacy matched war: the Amarna Letters show the pharaoh exchanging princesses and gold with Babylon, Assyria, and the Hittites, addressed as brothers, in the first fully documented great-power system in history. Akhenaten's revolution failed partly because it neglected this system: while the king worshipped the Aten, vassal letters begged in vain for troops as the empire frayed. The Nineteenth Dynasty restored the balance, and the treaty with the Hittites after Kadesh, sealed by the marriage of Ramesses II to a Hittite princess, fixed spheres of influence in terms recognizably modern; a copy of it hangs today at the United Nations.

The late New Kingdom also shows how empires die: the cost of wars, the corruption of officials, the strikes of unpaid tomb workers in Year 29 of Ramesses III, and the growing independence of the high priests of Amun, who ended by ruling Thebes as a state within the state, until the Two Lands drifted apart again into the Third Intermediate Period.
pageData.para2:
Empire transformed Egyptian society. Tribute and plunder from Nubian gold mines and Asian vassals poured into the temples of Amun at Karnak and Luxor, until the priesthood of Amun controlled vast estates and eventually rivaled the crown itself. A new class of professional soldiers rose, rewarded with land, and scribes administered an imperial bureaucracy that corresponded with Babylon, Assyria, and the Hittites in Akkadian cuneiform, the diplomatic language of the age. The Amarna Letters, clay tablets from Pharaoh's archive, preserve this correspondence, including pleading letters from Canaanite princes. Women in Egypt already enjoyed unusual legal standing for the ancient world: they could own property, initiate lawsuits, and make wills, and Hatshepsut showed a woman could even wear the double crown. Burial practice changed too.

Instead of conspicuous pyramids, New Kingdom pharaohs hid their tombs in the Valley of the Kings, deep rock-cut corridors painted with funerary texts such as the Book of the Dead. Art reached new heights, from the graceful realism of Thutmose's sculpture workshops, which produced the famous bust of Nefertiti, to the strange, elongated naturalism of the Amarna style and the intimate scenes of Akhenaten playing with his daughters. We know daily life unusually well because the village of the royal tomb builders, Deir el-Medina, survives with its houses, laundry lists, love songs, legal disputes, and even records of history's first documented labor strike, when workers downed tools over late grain rations under Ramesses III. Religious life grew both grander and more personal: great festivals filled the calendar, and ordinary people prayed directly to the gods for help with sickness and injustice.

The New Kingdom was ancient Egypt at its richest and most powerful, and its decline showed that even the greatest empire depends on solvency, succession, and order at home.

pageData.title: Sumer
pageData.para1:
Sumer. In the southern plain of Iraq, between and below the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, the world's first civilization took shape. The land was flat and dry, but the rivers flooded unpredictably, so survival depended on cooperation: communities that dug and maintained canals could turn the plain into the most fertile farmland on earth. By around 4000 BC villages were growing into towns, and by 3300 BC Uruk had become something entirely new, a true city of perhaps 40,000 people, centered on great temples such as the White Temple raised on its platform. Sumer was never a single kingdom but a patchwork of independent city-states: Uruk, Ur, Lagash, Kish, Umma, Nippur, Eridu, and others, each with its own patron god, its own temple estates, and its own ruler, who styled himself en or lugal and led both war and worship.

During the Early Dynastic period, roughly 2900 to 2350 BC, these cities competed fiercely for land, water, and prestige. The conflict between Lagash and Umma over a border field is recorded across generations of inscriptions, including the Stele of the Vultures, which shows King Eannatum's soldiers marching over their enemies. The Standard of Ur, a mosaic box found in the royal graves there, shows the two sides of city-state life on its two panels: war, with chariots and prisoners, and peace, with banquets, herds, and musicians. Around 2334 BC Sargon of Akkad, a Semitic-speaking ruler from the north, conquered the Sumerian cities one by one and forged the world's first territorial empire, which his grandson Naram-Sin pushed to its height. Akkadian rule lasted about a century and a half before collapsing under pressure from Gutian tribes.

Sumer rose once more in the Third Dynasty of Ur, when Ur-Nammu and his son Shulgi ran a tightly organized bureaucratic state, built the great ziggurat of Ur, and issued law codes. Around 2004 BC Elamites from Iran sacked Ur and carried off its king, and Sumerian political independence ended forever, though its culture outlived it. The archaeology of the plain tells the same story the tablets do. At Eridu, seventeen temples were built one on top of another across three thousand years, the oldest continuously used sacred site in the region, showing how the shrine grew into the city. At Uruk, excavators found the world's first mass-produced pottery, beveled-rim bowls used to ration grain to workers, proof that the city fed a labor force on an industrial scale.

The royal cemetery of Ur, dug in the 1920s, revealed the wealth and the terror of the city-state: Queen Puabi was buried in gold and lapis with a lyre, a sledge, and the bodies of dozens of attendants who followed their ruler in death. Sumerian kingship was understood as a gift from the gods, lowered from heaven, and it passed from city to city as the gods willed, an idea that let many small states share one civilization while fighting for its leadership. The economy of the temples and palaces organized irrigation on a scale no family could manage, and the word of the ruler who controlled the canals was law because water was life. Sumer also knew political experiment: the assembly of elders, and in Uruk a second assembly of fighting men, appear in the epic debating peace and war, the oldest recorded parliaments.

When Akkadian and later Babylonian kings ruled the land, they came to Sumerian Nippur for the blessing of Enlil, because legitimacy in Iraq remained Sumerian long after Sumer itself was gone.
pageData.para2:
Sumer's greatest invention was writing. It began around 3300 BC as accounting: temple officials pressed tokens and then wedge-shaped marks into clay tablets to record deliveries of barley, beer, oil, and sheep. The cuneiform script, written with a cut reed, gradually gained signs for sounds and ideas, until scribes could record anything: contracts, hymns, proverbs, letters, mathematics, and literature. Learning the script took years in the tablet house, the edubba, and the scribe who mastered it entered a privileged profession. Religion structured every city. Each city belonged to a patron god whose temple was the largest landowner and employer, and the temple's stepped tower, the ziggurat, rose as an artificial mountain dominating the city.

From Sumerian clay comes the world's first great work of literature, the Epic of Gilgamesh, in which the king of Uruk seeks eternal life, survives adventures, loses his friend Enkidu, and learns that immortality is not for mortals; its flood story is the oldest known version of a tale retold across later cultures. Sumerians also wrote the first law collections: Urukagina of Lagash boasts of reforms against corrupt officials, and Ur-Nammu's code sets fixed penalties in money for injuries, centuries before Hammurabi. The economy ran on barley and wool; temples organized spinning and weaving on an industrial scale, and traders traveled far because the plain had no metal, stone, or good timber, importing copper from Oman, tin from far to the east, timber from Lebanon. Sumerian mathematics used a base-sixty system, which is why we still divide hours into sixty minutes and circles into 360 degrees.

The wheel, the plow, the sailboat, the potter's wheel, and the first schools all appear here. Babylon and Assyria inherited Sumerian gods, literature, law, and learning, so that when later Iraqis studied the past, they studied Sumer.

pageData.title: Babylon
pageData.para1:
Babylon. After the fall of Ur around 2004 BC, southern Iraq fragmented among competing Amorite dynasties, and for two centuries no power dominated. The city of Babylon, on the Euphrates where the two rivers run closest together, was just one modest Amorite kingdom among rivals like Larsa, Eshnunna, Mari, and the great northern power of Assyria. Everything changed under Babylon's sixth king, Hammurabi, who reigned from about 1792 to 1750 BC. For three decades he governed patiently, building canals, temples, and alliances, defeating enemies one at a time rather than all at once. Then, in the last fourteen years of his reign, he struck: he defeated his former ally Rim-Sin of Larsa, conquered Mari and destroyed its magnificent palace, humbled Eshnunna, and forced even Assyria to submit, uniting all of Mesopotamia under Babylon for the first time since Ur.

Hammurabi is remembered above all for his law code, nearly three hundred laws carved in cuneiform on a black stone stele topped by a scene of the king receiving authority from Shamash, the sun god and god of justice. The code regulated prices, wages, marriage, inheritance, slavery, medicine, building standards, and agriculture, and it famously scaled punishments by social class: an injury to a noble cost more than the same injury to a commoner. It was not the first law code, but it was the most complete to survive, and its principle that the state publicly declares the law, so that the strong may not oppress the weak, echoes through all later legal history. After Hammurabi his empire slowly shrank, and around 1595 BC the Hittites marched down the Euphrates, sacked Babylon, and withdrew, leaving the Kassites, a people from the Zagros mountains, to rule Babylon for four centuries.

Babylon rose again under Nebuchadnezzar I around 1125 BC, then endured long Assyrian domination until the Chaldean Nabopolassar and his son Nebuchadnezzar II destroyed Assyria, with the Medes, between 616 and 609 BC. Nebuchadnezzar II rebuilt Babylon into the wonder of the world: the blue-glazed Ishtar Gate, the Processional Way, the great ziggurat Etemenanki, and, by later tradition, the Hanging Gardens. His empire fell in 539 BC when Cyrus the Persian entered Babylon without a battle. The reign of Hammurabi is documented not only by his law code but by hundreds of his letters, which show a king managing everything personally: assigning fields, investigating corrupt judges, ordering the repair of canals, and reminding governors that the water must flow. Irrigation was the state's first duty, and the code itself sets penalties for the farmer who neglects his dikes and floods his neighbor's field.

The stele's prologue declares that Hammurabi was chosen by the gods to cause justice to prevail and to destroy the wicked, so that the strong should not oppress the weak, a statement of the purpose of law that still reads as a charter of government. After the Kassite centuries, when Babylon was respected as the ancient holy city even by its foreign rulers, the Assyrian period tested Babylonian identity: the city rebelled again and again, was destroyed by Sennacherib and rebuilt by Esarhaddon, and finally led the coalition that destroyed Assyria itself. Nebuchadnezzar II's rebuilt capital, with walls wide enough, said the Greeks, for chariots to pass on top, was the marvel that travelers like Herodotus described; it was also the city of the Jewish exile, whose prophets and scholars, sitting by the rivers of Babylon, wrote some of the Bible's most famous words.

When Cyrus entered in 539 BC, his cylinder proclaimed in Babylonian tradition that he had come at Marduk's call to restore the sanctuaries and free the captives, and the exiles went home: Babylon had become the measure by which conquerors proved their worth.
pageData.para2:
Babylonian civilization was heir to Sumer and teacher to everyone after. Babylonian scholars studied the Sumerian language the way later students studied Latin, copying the Epic of Gilgamesh and the creation epic Enuma Elish, recited every New Year in honor of the city god Marduk. Religion centered on great temple households, and the temple of the city god Marduk, with its seven-story ziggurat, dominated the capital. Temple scholars kept nightly records of the heavens for centuries, believing the stars held signs, and from this long observation came Babylon's most influential science: astronomy. Its scholars discovered that eclipses and planetary motions repeat in calculable cycles, and invented mathematical astronomy so precise that Greek astronomers later borrowed its methods and data wholesale.

The Babylonian base-sixty number system, with place value and an early placeholder for zero, let them solve quadratic equations, calculate compound interest, and produce the tablet known as Plimpton 322, which lists what we now call Pythagorean triples a thousand years before Pythagoras. Our sixty-minute hour and 360-degree circle are Babylonian inheritance. The economy rested on irrigated barley and date palms, managed by temples and palaces but increasingly also by private merchant families like the Egibi, whose surviving archives show them financing trade, farming, and tax collection across generations. Society was stratified into free citizens, a dependent class, and slaves, with law fixing the rights and obligations of each; women could own property, run businesses, and appear in court, especially if they were priestesses or widows.

When Cyrus captured Babylon, he presented himself not as a destroyer but as Marduk's chosen restorer, and the city's temples, scholars, and astronomical diaries continued under Persian, Greek, and Parthian rule, making Babylon for fifteen hundred years the intellectual capital of the ancient world.

pageData.title: Assyria
pageData.para1:
Assyria. In the rain-fed hills of northern Iraq, around the cities of Ashur, Nineveh, Nimrud, and Khorsabad on the upper Tigris, rose the most formidable military state of the ancient world. Ashur began as a merchant city: in the early second millennium BC its traders ran caravan networks deep into Anatolia, exchanging tin and textiles for silver, and leaving thousands of business letters in the trading colony of Kanesh. The Middle Assyrian kings, from about 1360 BC, turned the city into a kingdom, taking advantage of Babylon's weakness to conquer northern Mesopotamia, and kings like Tukulti-Ninurta I even captured Babylon itself. After a period of decline under pressure from Aramean migrations, Assyria rebounded in the Neo-Assyrian Empire, beginning with Ashurnasirpal II around 883 BC, who moved the capital to Nimrud and advertised his power in palace reliefs and inscriptions that describe conquest in terrifying detail. Assyria's strength was organizational.

Its kings fielded the first great professional standing army, with iron weapons, siege engines that battered city walls, cavalry, engineers who diverted rivers, and an intelligence and supply system that could move armies hundreds of miles. Tiglath-Pileser III, who seized the throne in 745 BC, created the first true empire in the administrative sense: conquered lands were annexed as provinces under Assyrian governors, and subject peoples were deported in mass resettlements, moved across the empire to break their unity and repopulate devastated regions. His successors Sargon II, Sennacherib, Esarhaddon, and Ashurbanipal extended rule from Egypt, conquered by Esarhaddon in 671 BC, to Elam and the Persian Gulf. Sennacherib destroyed rebellious Babylon in 689 BC, an act of religious shock even to his own people; his son Esarhaddon rebuilt it. Ashurbanipal presided over the empire's cultural peak and its last conquests.

Then, with startling speed, it all collapsed: a coalition of Babylonians under Nabopolassar and Medes under Cyaxares destroyed Assyria between 616 and 609 BC, sacking Nineveh in 612. The empire had ruled so harshly and extracted so much that almost no one mourned it, and within a generation travelers reported its capitals as empty ruins. The empire's wars are documented in an unmatched archive: royal annals that list campaigns year by year, letters from spies and governors, and the palace reliefs that narrate sieges and deportations scene by scene. Ashurbanipal's campaign against Elam ended with the sack of Susa in 647 BC; that city was also where an Elamite king had carried off the stele of Hammurabi's laws as booty from Babylon some five centuries earlier, which is why it stands in the Louvre today.

Assyrian policy toward Babylon was the empire's unsolvable problem: the ancient holy city could not be treated like a conquered town, yet it would not stop conspiring with Elam, and the kings alternated between ruling it directly, placing their brothers on its throne, and, in Sennacherib's case, razing it in fury, an act his own successors treated as sacrilege. The empire also met the west: Sargon II crushed a revolt at Ashdod, received tribute from Cyprus, and corresponded with the kingdom of Judah, and Sennacherib's siege of Jerusalem in 701 BC is recorded both in his annals and in the Bible, one of the rare ancient events we can read from both sides.

Assyrian kingship fused warrior and priest: the king campaigned almost every year of his reign, consulted the sun god's oracle before battles, and described himself as the shepherd of his peoples even while boasting of mountains of corpses. That contradiction, terror as policy and order as ideal, was the empire's genius and its doom, for it built a state that could conquer everything and reconcile nothing.
pageData.para2:
Assyria's reputation for cruelty was deliberate policy: royal inscriptions and palace reliefs described flaying, impalement, and mass deportation to spread terror in advance of the army, so that cities would surrender without a siege. Yet Assyria was far more than a war machine, and its daily civilization was sophisticated. The Assyrians were superb organizers: provincial governors reported to the king by fast courier, a relay postal system covered the empire, and standard weights, measures, and calendars kept taxation predictable. Mass deportation, brutal as it was, moved skilled craftsmen, farmers, and scribes across the empire, mixing peoples and spreading technologies; many deportees were settled as state farmers rather than enslaved. Religion remained Mesopotamian: the national god Ashur led the pantheon, and the king ruled as his priest and deputy, consulting diviners before campaigns. Assyrian scribes preserved Mesopotamian learning deliberately.

In his palace at Nineveh, Ashurbanipal assembled the ancient world's first systematically collected library, sending scholars across the land to copy tablets of omens, hymns, medical texts, and literature; more than twenty thousand tablets from his library survive, including the best-preserved copy of the Epic of Gilgamesh, and modern knowledge of Sumerian and Babylonian literature rests largely on it. Assyrian art reached a peak of narrative power: the alabaster reliefs of the palaces show the king hunting lions with bow and spear, armies storming cities, prisoners marched into exile, and banquets in gardens, carved with an eye for animal suffering that still moves viewers. Winged bull colossi with human heads guarded palace gates. The economy mixed agriculture in the northern rain zone with the tribute and trade of empire, and Assyrian law, preserved in the Middle Assyrian code, was notably severe, especially toward women, whose veiling it regulated by class.

Assyria bequeathed to the region its imperial model: provinces, deportation, courier roads, and royal ideology were inherited by Babylon, then Persia, and through them shaped how empires worked for a thousand years. The king lists, chronicles, and eponym calendars of Assyria also give modern historians the backbone of ancient Near Eastern chronology.

pageData.title: Minoan Crete
pageData.para1:
Minoan Crete. On the island of Crete, positioned in the eastern Mediterranean between Greece, Egypt, and Asia, Europe's first civilization flourished during the Bronze Age, from about 2000 to 1450 BC. We know it not from its own readable texts, since its main scripts remain undeciphered, but from its ruins and from later Greek legend, which remembered Crete as the realm of King Minos, his labyrinth, and the Minotaur. Around 1900 BC the Cretans began building great complexes that archaeologists call palaces, at Knossos, Phaistos, Malia, and Zakros. These were not royal fortresses but sprawling, unfortified centers of storage, craft production, ceremony, and administration, arranged around central courts, with light wells, colonnades, painted plaster, and sophisticated plumbing, including flushing drains at Knossos that had no equal in Europe for over three thousand years.

The palace at Knossos covered some thirteen thousand square meters, a maze of rooms that may have inspired the labyrinth legend. Around 1700 BC an earthquake destroyed the old palaces, but the Cretans rebuilt them grander than before, and the following century and a half was the Minoan golden age. Cretan ships dominated Aegean trade, carrying olive oil, wine, wool, and fine painted pottery to Egypt, where tomb paintings show Cretan envoys bearing gifts, to Syria, Cyprus, and the Greek mainland, where Minoan influence was so strong that later Greeks remembered paying tribute to Minos. Minoan settlers and trading posts spread across the Aegean islands, most spectacularly at Akrotiri on Thera, a town preserved in volcanic ash like a Bronze Age Pompeii, its houses decorated with frescoes of ships, fishermen, and saffron gatherers.

Around 1600 BC the volcano of Thera erupted in one of the largest explosions in human history, burying Akrotiri and sending tsunamis against Crete's north coast. The palaces survived, but the blow weakened the island. Around 1450 BC most Cretan palaces were destroyed by fire, and Greek-speaking Mycenaeans from the mainland took over Knossos, ruling it until the final collapse of the palace system around 1200 BC, when the whole Bronze Age world of the eastern Mediterranean came apart. The man who revealed this world was Arthur Evans, who began digging at Knossos in 1900 and named the civilization after the legendary king. Evans rebuilt parts of the palace in concrete, and his restorations, whatever their faults, fixed the world's image of Minoan Crete: grand staircases, light wells, red columns tapering downward, and walls brilliant with frescoes.

The palace archives show the system's workings: Linear A tablets record contributions of wine, oil, figs, and wool to the palace stores, and the great magazines, lined with jars taller than a man, held the agricultural wealth of the countryside, from which the palace fed workers, supplied feasts, and financed trade. Crete's position made it the natural middleman of the eastern Mediterranean: Egyptian scarabs and stone vessels reached Knossos, and Minoan pottery has been found from the Nile Delta to Syria, Cyprus, and mainland Greece, while Keftiu, as the Egyptians called the Cretans, appear in Theban tomb paintings carrying metal ingots and elaborate vessels.

Society seems to have been organized around the palaces and their festivals rather than around warrior kings: there are no royal portraits, no boasting inscriptions, and almost no fortifications, which suggests either an unusual peace among the Cretan cities or a thalassocracy, a sea-power, that kept enemies away. The Thera eruption, dated around 1600 BC, was among the largest volcanic events of the last ten thousand years, and some have linked its memory to Plato's tale of Atlantis; whether or not that is true, the blow to Cretan shipping and harvests opened the door to the Mycenaean Greeks, whose takeover is visible in the sudden appearance of Linear B, warrior graves, and Greek names in the last century of Knossos.
pageData.para2:
Minoan society remains mysterious because we cannot yet read its main scripts, Cretan hieroglyphic and Linear A, though the later Linear B, used by the Mycenaean rulers of Knossos, was deciphered as early Greek and reveals a palace bureaucracy tracking flocks, grain, oil, and workers in meticulous detail. What the art shows is a culture strikingly different from its warlike neighbors: Minoan walls carry almost no scenes of battle or kings. Instead the frescoes glow with leaping dolphins, flowering lilies, octopuses coiling across pottery, and elegant figures in flounced skirts.

The most famous images show the bull-leaping ritual, in which young men and women grasped the horns of a charging bull and somersaulted over its back, perhaps a religious ceremony, perhaps a sport, probably both; the bull's importance may echo in the Minotaur legend, and the massive bull's-head rhyta and horns of consecration found at the palaces confirm the animal's sacred status. Religion centered on goddesses and sacred symbols such as the double axe and the bull, worshipped at mountaintop shrines, caves, and palace sanctuaries; strikingly, no statues of rulers have been found. Priests or priestesses seem to have led the ceremonies. The economy rested on the palace storage system: giant jars held oil, wine, and grain collected as dues from the countryside and redistributed to workers and craftspeople. Minoan craftsmen made exquisite seal stones, gold jewelry, carved stone vases, and the eggshell-thin Kamares pottery traded across the Mediterranean.

Women appear prominently in Minoan art and ritual, leading some scholars to suggest they held unusually high status, though without readable texts we cannot know how the society was governed or whether a king like the legendary Minos ever existed. When the Mycenaean Greeks conquered Crete, they absorbed Minoan art, religion, and administrative methods, and through them Minoan influence flowed into Greek civilization: the first Europeans, in a real sense, were the Cretans.

pageData.title: Athens
pageData.para1:
Classical Athens. In the fifth century BC, a small Greek city-state produced an explosion of political experiment, art, and thought that has shaped the world ever since. Athens had already pioneered reform: Solon's laws in 594 BC canceled debts and ended debt slavery, and Cleisthenes in 508 BC reorganized the citizens into new tribes and created the Council of Five Hundred, laying the foundation of democracy. The Persian Wars made Athens a great power. When the Persian Empire invaded Greece, the Athenians defeated Darius at Marathon in 490 BC, and ten years later, under Themistocles, their new fleet destroyed Xerxes' navy at Salamis, the decisive battle of the war.

Afterward Athens led the Delian League, a voluntary alliance of Greek cities formed to keep fighting Persia, but gradually turned the alliance into an empire: the treasury was moved from Delos to Athens, allies who tried to leave were forced back, and tribute paid for Athenian ships and buildings. Under Pericles, the dominant statesman from about 461 to 429 BC, democracy reached its fullest form. Every male citizen could speak and vote in the Assembly, which met about forty times a year; juries of hundreds, chosen by lot and paid for their service, judged cases; most officials were selected by lottery rather than election, on the principle that any citizen could govern. Pericles used league funds to rebuild the Acropolis, crowned by the Parthenon between 447 and 432 BC, a temple to Athena of perfect proportions filled with sculpture directed by Phidias.

Democracy and empire together funded the golden age of Athenian culture. But imperial arrogance bred enemies, and in 431 BC the long rivalry with Sparta erupted into the Peloponnesian War. Pericles' strategy of withdrawing behind the city walls packed refugees into Athens, where plague killed perhaps a quarter of the population, including Pericles himself. The war ground on for twenty-seven years, marked by the disastrous Sicilian expedition of 415 to 413 BC, in which Athens lost an entire army and fleet. In 404 BC Athens surrendered to Sparta, its walls demolished and its empire gone, though its democracy, twice overthrown by oligarchic coups, was twice restored, and its cultural influence only grew after its political fall. The democracy's machinery deserves close attention, because it was the most participatory government of the ancient world.

The Assembly met on the Pnyx hill, and any citizen could speak; decrees required thousands of votes; the Council of Five Hundred, chosen by lot for a single year, prepared business and ran daily administration; and the courts, with juries of hundreds chosen by lot each morning, were the final guardians of the law, since no appeal and no professional judiciary stood above them. Citizens could even vote once a year to exile, without trial, any man they judged too powerful: the ostracism, for which votes were scratched on potsherds that archaeologists still find.

The empire paid for this system and for the fleet that defended it, and the tension between democracy at home and domination abroad runs through everything Athens did: the allies became subjects, the treasury moved to Athens, and Pericles frankly told the Assembly that the empire was like a tyranny, perhaps unjust to take but dangerous to let go. The golden age was also the age of construction: besides the Parthenon, the Propylaea gateway, the Erechtheum with its maidens, and the temple of Nike rose on the Acropolis in a generation, while the fleet of two hundred triremes, rowed by the poor citizens who thereby gained political weight, made Athens mistress of the sea.

The Peloponnesian War revealed the system's flaws and strengths alike: the Assembly could vote the catastrophic Sicilian expedition in a surge of enthusiasm and condemn its own generals in a fit of anger, yet it also sustained the war effort for a generation and twice restored democracy after oligarchic coups. Athens fell, but its argument, that ordinary citizens can govern themselves, never died.
pageData.para2:
Athenian democracy was direct, not representative: the Assembly of adult male citizens made every major decision, from declaring war to taxing the rich, and power rotated so widely that a citizen might serve on the Council, judge in the courts, and preside over the Assembly within his lifetime. Yet the citizen body was a minority of the population. Women were excluded from politics and lived largely in domestic seclusion; resident foreigners, the metics, paid taxes and served in the army without citizenship; and a large enslaved population, including the wretched miners of Laurion whose silver paid for the fleet, did much of the hard labor. The democracy was also a school of speech and thought. In the agora, the marketplace and civic heart, citizens debated, shopped, and argued philosophy.

Socrates walked there questioning everyone about justice and virtue until the democracy, shaken by war, condemned him to death in 399 BC for impiety and corrupting the young; his student Plato founded the Academy and wrote dialogues that made Socrates immortal, and Plato's student Aristotle founded the Lyceum and systematized logic, ethics, politics, and biology, becoming the teacher of Alexander the Great and the authority of later ages. Athens invented tragedy and comedy: Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides staged dramas of fate, pride, and suffering at the festival of Dionysus, while Aristophanes mocked politicians and philosophers in savage comedies. Herodotus, who lived in Athens, wrote the first history, an inquiry into the Persian Wars, and Thucydides followed with a ruthlessly analytical account of the Peloponnesian War that remains a manual of power politics.

Athenian potters painted the red-figure vases found from Etruria to the Black Sea, and Athenian architects and sculptors set the classical standard of balanced, idealized form. When modern republics deliberate in assemblies, when courts use citizen juries, when we stage plays or ask what justice is, we are walking paths first cut in classical Athens, whose people, as Pericles' funeral speech claimed, made their city an education to Greece.

pageData.title: Sparta
pageData.para1:
Sparta. In the Eurotas valley of Laconia, in the southern Peloponnese, the Greeks built a society unlike any other: a citizen body of full-time soldiers ruling over a conquered population many times its size. The system emerged after the Spartans conquered neighboring Messenia in the eighth and seventh centuries BC and reduced its people to helots, state-owned serfs bound to the land, who farmed to feed their Spartan masters. Fear of helot revolt shaped everything. According to tradition the lawgiver Lycurgus remade Sparta into a military camp: land was divided into equal lots worked by helots, wealth display was banned, iron bars served as money to discourage trade, and the whole male citizenry lived for war.

Government balanced several powers: two hereditary kings led the army, a council of elders over sixty proposed laws, the assembly of citizens voted, and five annually elected overseers, the ephors, wielded enormous power, including the right to declare war on the helots each year so they could be killed without religious pollution. Spartan education, the agoge, took boys from their families at seven and raised them in herds, deliberately underfed and underclothed, taught to steal food but punished savagely if caught, hardened by endurance contests and ritual floggings, and trained above all in obedience and fighting. The result was the finest infantry in Greece, the heavy-armed hoplites whose unbreakable shield line won battle after battle.

At Thermopylae in 480 BC, King Leonidas and three hundred Spartans held the pass against the Persian army to the death, a sacrifice that became Greece's legend of courage; the next year Sparta led the allied victory at Plataea that ended the invasion. After the Persian Wars, Spartan power and suspicion of Athens produced the Peloponnesian War, which Sparta finally won in 404 BC with Persian money and the admiral Lysander's fleet. But victory destroyed Sparta's balance: garrisons and governors spread across Greece bred corruption and resentment, the citizen body shrank as land concentrated in few hands, and after the defeat by Thebes at Leuctra in 371 BC, the helots of Messenia were liberated and Sparta's economic base was gone. It lingered for centuries as a museum of its own customs, but its real history ended there. Sparta's origins explain its later shape.

The Spartans were Dorian-speaking Greeks who settled Laconia and, unlike other city-states, solved their land hunger not by sending out colonies but by conquering their neighbors and enslaving them wholesale, first in Laconia and then in Messenia. The result was a permanent state of siege disguised as a constitution: every institution was bent to keep a few thousand citizens dominant over a helot population perhaps seven times their number. The famous laconic speech, the Spartans trained boys to answer briefly and pointedly, and the word survives in our language, was the style of men who feared saying too much. Their army's superiority was real and systematic: where other Greeks farmed and drilled occasionally, Spartans drilled constantly, marched in step to the flute, and maneuvered formations no amateur phalanx could match, so that for two centuries a Spartan army in the field was assumed invincible.

Thermopylae became the myth of that system at its best: Leonidas, knowing the oracle that Sparta must lose a king or fall, stayed to die with his three hundred, and the inscription over their graves, telling the passerby to report that they died obeying Sparta's laws, is the most famous epitaph of the ancient world. Yet the system consumed itself: citizenship depended on contributing to the common mess from one's land, and as land concentrated through inheritance and marriage, whole families fell out of the citizen body until Sparta, which had fielded eight thousand hoplites at Plataea, could muster barely a thousand by the time of Leuctra. Thebes' victory freed Messenia after three centuries, and the liberated helots built their own city at Messene, whose walls still stand: the foundation of Sparta's power was removed, and no reform ever replaced it.
pageData.para2:
Spartan society was divided into three rigid orders. At the top stood the Spartiates, the full citizens, perhaps eight thousand men at their peak, forbidden to farm, trade, or work with their hands, their lives devoted to exercise, drilling, and the common messes where they dined together on the famous black broth. Below them were the perioikoi, the dwellers-around, free inhabitants of Laconia's towns who conducted the trade and craftwork the citizens scorned and served in the army without political rights. At the bottom were the helots, who vastly outnumbered their masters and were treated with calculated brutality; the young men of the secret police, the krypteia, were sent out to kill the strongest of them. The system worked because it made Sparta a permanently armed camp: every citizen was a soldier from seven to sixty, and the army's discipline was legendary.

Yet the same system carried the seeds of decline. Citizens who lost their land lots lost their status, so the citizen body steadily shrank until the army could no longer be replaced. Spartan women were unusual in Greece: they trained in running and wrestling, could inherit and control land, and were famous for their plain speech; a Spartan mother was said to hand her son his shield with the words, with it or on it. Because men spent their lives in barracks and campaigns, women managed estates, and by the fourth century BC much of Sparta's land was in female hands. Culture in the wider sense was deliberately rejected: Sparta produced no philosophers, no historians, almost no art after the austere early centuries, and its oracle-bound religion and moon-timed campaigns sometimes paralyzed its strategy.

What Sparta did produce was a political idea that has fascinated the world ever since: the mixed constitution balancing kings, elders, and people, which Greeks like Plato and Aristotle studied as a model of stability, and which later thinkers saw as a forerunner of balanced government. Athens showed what freedom and talent could create; Sparta showed what discipline and equality of sacrifice could endure, and the tension between the two models has never ceased to shape political debate.

pageData.title: Early Japan (Kofun & Asuka)
pageData.para1:
Early Japan. The Japanese islands were settled in the Ice Age, and by about 10,000 BC their inhabitants were making some of the oldest pottery in the world, the cord-marked vessels of the Jomon people, hunter-gatherers who lived in settled villages of pit houses for thousands of years, an unusually stable Stone Age culture. Everything changed around 300 BC, when rice farming arrived from the Asian mainland, probably through Korea, bringing the Yayoi period. Wet-rice agriculture demanded cooperation to build and maintain paddies and channels, and with it came bronze bells, iron tools, social ranking, and warfare between small chiefdoms. Chinese chronicles of the third century AD describe a land of many small countries, some ruled by queens, including the shaman-queen Himiko of Yamatai, who sent tribute missions to China.

In the following Kofun period, roughly 250 to 600 AD, power gathered in the Yamato plain, where rulers built enormous keyhole-shaped burial mounds surrounded by moats and lined with clay figures, the largest, attributed to Emperor Nintoku, covering more ground than the Great Pyramid of Giza. From these tombs, and from Chinese records, we see a warrior aristocracy of horse-riding clans, organized into hereditary guilds, gradually unifying the islands under the Yamato court, from which Japan's imperial line claims unbroken descent to this day. The sixth and seventh centuries brought deliberate transformation. Buddhism arrived from Korea in 538 or 552, championed by the Soga clan against conservative rivals, and with it came Chinese writing, calendar science, medicine, and statecraft.

Prince Shotoku, regent from 593, issued the Seventeen-Article Constitution, a set of moral and administrative precepts modeled on Chinese ideals of centralized, virtuous rule, and sent embassies directly to China's Sui court, famously addressing the Chinese emperor as an equal, from the land of the rising sun to the land of the setting sun. In 645 the Taika Reforms abolished private clan control of land and people, declaring all land the emperor's, and established Chinese-style taxation and provinces. Japan was deliberately remaking itself as a centralized state on the Chinese model, though always adapting what it borrowed to its own conditions. The sources for this age are unusually revealing, because Japan enters history through foreign eyes.

Chinese dynastic histories record the tribute missions of the third century and describe the Yamatai kingdom of Queen Himiko, who ruled through shamanic trance and was buried, the chronicle says, in a great mound with a hundred sacrificed attendants, a detail matched by the keyhole tombs then rising in Japan. The kofun themselves, built from the third to the sixth century, mark the growth of royal power: the largest mounds required the labor of thousands, and their contents, armor, horse gear, mirrors, and jewels from Korea and China, show both a horse-riding warrior elite and deep ties to the mainland. Korea was the bridge: the Yamato court kept a foothold on the peninsula, and waves of Korean and Chinese immigrants, scribes, weavers, smiths, and potters, brought the skills of the continent and were organized into the service guilds of the court.

The sixth century decided Japan's direction: when the Soga championed Buddhism against the Mononobe and Nakatomi, who defended the native gods, the victory of the Soga at the battle of Shigisan in 587 opened the road to continental civilization on a grand scale. Prince Shotoku's constitution ordered officials to prize harmony and to obey the imperial will, and his embassies to Sui China brought back students who spent decades studying the Chinese state and returned to run the reforms. The Taika coup of 645 destroyed the Soga, and the reform edicts that followed abolished private ownership of people and land, established registers and taxes on the Chinese model, and built a capital in imitation of the Chinese grid. Japan was one of history's great examples of a nation remaking itself by deliberate imitation, and it would repeat the performance, on a far larger scale, after 1868.
pageData.para2:
Early Japanese society was built on clans, the uji, each claiming descent from a divine or heroic ancestor, each controlling its own lands and its hereditary corporations of farmers, weavers, potters, and soldiers. The Yamato ruler was first among clan chiefs rather than an absolute emperor, and legitimacy came from sacred descent: the imperial line traced itself to the sun goddess Amaterasu, whose shrine at Ise became the holiest site of Japan's native religion. That religion, later called Shinto, honored the spirits of nature and ancestors at shrines across the land, and Japan's first written histories, the Kojiki of 712 and the Nihon Shoki of 720, placed the imperial house at the center of its myths, giving the throne sacred legitimacy.

When Buddhism arrived from the mainland, it blended with these older practices rather than replacing them, and temples and shrines stood side by side, a pattern that still defines Japanese life. The economy centered on rice, which was wealth itself: taxes were assessed in sheaves, and control of wet-paddy land was the foundation of every clan's power. Iron tools, Chinese and Korean immigrant craftsmen, and new techniques spread silk weaving, glazed pottery, and roof tiles. Japan in this period had no cities on the mainland scale, no coinage in daily use, and no writing of its own; it imported all three. Chinese characters were adapted to write Japanese, a complex marriage of two utterly different languages that produced the mixed script Japan still uses.

The great achievement of the age was selective borrowing: Japan took Chinese law codes, bureaucracy, Buddhism, city planning, and writing, but left out the Chinese examination system and the idea that heaven transfers the mandate to rule between dynasties; in Japan the imperial line was eternal, a flexibility that let real power pass to regents and shoguns in later centuries while the throne endured. The Kofun and Asuka ages thus laid the foundations on which Nara, Heian, and all later Japan would build.

pageData.title: The Rashidun Caliphate
pageData.para1:
The Rashidun Caliphate. When the Prophet Muhammad died in 632, he left a young Muslim community in Arabia with no agreed rule of succession and no precedent for leading a state. The community's elders chose Abu Bakr, the Prophet's close companion and father-in-law, as the first caliph, meaning successor. His two-year reign faced immediate crisis: tribes across Arabia renounced allegiance or followed rival prophets, and Abu Bakr fought the Ridda wars, the wars of apostasy, to reunite the peninsula under Islam. Under his rule and his brilliant general Khalid ibn al-Walid, Muslim armies then moved beyond Arabia almost accidentally, raiding into Iraq and Syria, and found the two exhausted superpowers of the age, the Byzantine and Sasanian empires, unable to stop them. Umar ibn al-Khattab, caliph from 634 to 644, presided over the astonishing decade of conquest.

In 636 his armies destroyed the Byzantine field army at Yarmouk and took Syria, and Jerusalem surrendered the next year; in the same years the Sasanian army was shattered at Qadisiyyah, and by 651 the whole Persian Empire had fallen. Egypt was conquered by Amr ibn al-As between 639 and 642, and within a single generation Muslim rule stretched from Libya to the borders of Central Asia. Umar organized the new empire: garrison cities such as Fustat in Egypt, Kufa and Basra in Iraq were founded, a register divided stipends from conquest revenue among the Muslim soldiers and their families, and the calendar was fixed from the Hijra of 622. Conquered peoples kept their lands and religions as protected subjects paying tribute, an arrangement that made conquest cheaper and, at first, made few demands for conversion.

Umar was assassinated by a Persian slave in 644, and Uthman ibn Affan, of the powerful Umayyad clan, continued the expansion while standardizing the text of the Quran into the single official recension still used today. But charges of favoritism toward his clan grew, rebellious soldiers from Egypt and Iraq besieged his house in Medina, and in 656 he was murdered. Ali, the Prophet's cousin and son-in-law, became the fourth caliph amid civil war: he fought the Battle of the Camel against Aisha and other opponents, then faced the revolt of Muawiya, governor of Syria, whose standoff at Siffin ended in arbitration. A breakaway faction, the Kharijites, assassinated Ali in 661. Muawiya took the caliphate, and the age of the elected Rightly Guided caliphs gave way to hereditary empire. The speed of the conquests still astonishes historians, and several causes worked together.

The Byzantine and Sasanian empires had just fought each other to exhaustion in a generation-long war, and the peoples of Syria, Egypt, and Iraq, many of them Christians at odds with Constantinople's orthodoxy, or Jews and peasants crushed by taxation, often found Muslim rule lighter than the old. The Arab armies were superbly led and highly motivated, fighting with the confidence of a new faith and the experience of desert war; Khalid ibn al-Walid's march across the desert from Iraq to Syria in 634 remains a legend of military daring. Equally important, the conquerors did not at first seek to convert or to settle among the conquered: they built garrison cities apart, kept the existing tax systems running in Greek and Persian, and protected churches, synagogues, and fire temples in return for tribute, so that local elites found cooperation rational.

Umar's settlement was the foundation: the conquest revenue was shared among the Muslim soldiers by a fixed register of stipends, the caliph keeping only a fifth for the community's needs, and land was left in the hands of its cultivators rather than divided among the conquerors. This made the empire a tax state ruling subject peoples rather than a colony of settlers, and it held for a century. The civil wars at the end of the period fixed the great questions: whether the community should be led by the most meritorious, as the first caliphs claimed, or by the Prophet's kin, as Ali's party insisted; and whether a ruler who governs unjustly forfeits obedience. Those arguments, born in the murders of Uthman and Ali and the martyrdom of Husayn at Karbala under the dynasty that followed, shaped Sunni and Shia Islam and are still alive today.
pageData.para2:
The Rashidun era asks the deepest question in Islamic history: how should the community be led after the Prophet? The first caliphs ruled not as kings but as successors to the Prophet's political role, guarding the community, commanding the armies, and judging disputes, while making no claim to prophecy. They consulted senior companions, governed from modest houses, and in Umar's legendary image walked the streets of Medina checking on the poor. Their authority rested on personal piety, election by the community's leading men, and success in war. The conquests created a new social order. Arab Muslim soldiers settled in new garrison towns, kept apart from the conquered populations, living off stipends from the tribute of subject peoples, who remained Christian, Jewish, Zoroastrian, or otherwise and paid taxes for protection and exemption from military service.

Administration at first stayed in local hands: Greek and Persian scribes kept their posts, coins and tax systems continued, and life for most farmers changed little beyond the name of the ruler. Yet the empire's very success strained the old Arabian equality. Conquest enriched some families far beyond others; Uthman's relatives filled the governorships; and the first civil war split the community along lines that have endured: those who upheld the legitimacy of the first three caliphs and Muawiya's succession, who became the Sunni majority, and those who held that leadership belonged to Ali and the Prophet's family, who became the Shia. The murder of Uthman and the killing of Ali planted the question of whether rebellion against an unjust ruler can ever be right, while the Kharijites answered with a violence that horrified everyone else.

In this crucible the institutions of Islamic civilization were forged: the caliphate itself, the Quran's fixed text, the early schools of law and tradition in Medina, Kufa, and Basra, and the memory of a rightly guided age against which every later Muslim reformer, down to the present, has measured his own time.

pageData.title: The Umayyad Caliphate
pageData.para1:
The Umayyad Caliphate. When Muawiya ibn Abi Sufyan became caliph in 661, he moved the capital from Medina to Damascus, his longtime power base as governor of Syria, and founded Islam's first dynasty, ruling until 750. Muawiya governed with patient pragmatism: he kept the experienced Arab tribal armies of Syria loyal, left the old Byzantine tax administration in place, and built the caliphate into a durable state. His most fateful act came at the end: he secured the succession for his son Yazid, turning the caliphate into a hereditary monarchy. Yazid's reign was scarred by the event that has echoed through Islamic memory ever since. In 680, Husayn, the Prophet's grandson, set out to claim the caliphate and was intercepted at Karbala in Iraq, where he and his small band of relatives and followers were killed by Umayyad forces.

The martyrdom of Husayn became the founding grief of Shia Islam, mourned to this day. After a second civil war, the Umayyads recovered under Abd al-Malik, caliph from 685 to 705, the true organizer of the empire. He made Arabic the language of administration, replacing Greek and Persian; minted the first distinctively Islamic coinage, bearing Quranic verses instead of images; and crowned Jerusalem with the Dome of the Rock, completed in 691, the oldest surviving monument of Islamic architecture, built over the rock sacred to Jews and Muslims. His son al-Walid carried the empire to its greatest extent. Between 711 and 718 Muslim armies conquered most of Spain, crossed the Pyrenees, took Transoxiana beyond the Oxus river, and reached the Indus valley in Sind.

In barely a century the caliphate had grown from Arabia into the largest empire the world had yet seen, stretching from the Atlantic to the borders of China. But expansion carried its own undoing. The empire was run by and for the Arab Muslim military aristocracy, while the growing numbers of non-Arab converts to Islam, the mawali, found themselves treated as second-class Muslims, still taxed like subjects. Resentment burned hottest in Iraq and Iran, and Umayyad armies were worn down fighting Berbers in North Africa and Byzantines on the Anatolian frontier. In 750 the Abbasid revolution, launched from eastern Iran under the black banners, destroyed the dynasty; only one prince, Abd al-Rahman I, escaped, fleeing across North Africa to found a new Umayyad emirate in Spain, which would flourish there for centuries.

The dynasty's politics ran through two rival centers: Medina, where the memory of the Prophet and the grievances of the old families lived, and Damascus, where Muawiya had built a Syrian army loyal to his house. The second civil war after Muawiya's death nearly destroyed the dynasty: Ibn al-Zubayr ruled Mecca and much of the empire for a decade, Kharijite rebels burned through Arabia and Iraq, and Shia risings, first the Tawwabun mourning Husayn, then the revolt of al-Mukhtar avenging him, convulsed Iraq, until Abd al-Malik's general al-Hajjaj reconquered the province and governed it for twenty years with an iron hand, becoming the very type of the harsh governor in Arabic memory.

The conquests under al-Walid were the work of a generation of brilliant commanders: Tariq crossed the strait that bears his name, Gibraltar, in 711 and broke Visigothic Spain; Qutayba carried Arab rule to Samarkand and Bukhara; Muhammad ibn al-Qasim conquered Sind. The empire these men built faced a problem no earlier state had solved: how to rule peoples who vastly outnumbered the conquerors and who were now converting to the conquerors' faith. The pious caliph Umar II, who reigned briefly from 717, tried to equalize converts and Arabs and to govern justly, and is honored as the fifth rightly guided caliph, but the fiscal logic of empire defeated him.

The Abbasid movement exploited exactly this: preaching in Iran that the dynasty had betrayed the equality of Islam, it drew Arab settlers, Persian converts, and Shia sympathizers into one coalition, and the armies from Khurasan that took Iraq in 749 were the instrument of that coalition. The Umayyads fell because they ruled a Muslim society as an Arab kingdom, a lesson their successors professed to have learned.
pageData.para2:
Under the Umayyads, Islam became the civilization of a world empire rather than the faith of Arabian conquerors. Damascus, ancient and rich, gave the caliphs a palace court very different from the austere circle of Medina: poets praised the caliph and lampooned his enemies, secretaries ran bureaus of taxation and correspondence, and the desert palaces that survive in Jordan, with their frescoes, baths, and hunting scenes, show rulers enjoying wine, music, and the chase in ways pious critics condemned as worldly. Yet this was also the age that gave Islam its enduring visual identity.

With Arabic as the single language of government and the Quran as its sacred text, and with figural images excluded from religious settings, artists developed the characteristic Islamic repertoire of calligraphy, geometric pattern, and arabesque, most gloriously in the Dome of the Rock, whose golden dome and mosaic splendor proclaimed the new faith in the city Jews and Christians also held holy, and in the Great Mosque of Damascus, with its glittering mosaics of paradise. Society was layered. At the top stood the Arab Muslim elite of the garrison cities, registered for stipends; below them the mawali, non-Arab converts attached to Arab tribes as clients; then the protected peoples, Christians, Jews, and Zoroastrians, who paid tribute and kept their own religious law; and at the bottom the enslaved, many captured in the wars.

Most people farmed as before, in Egypt's Nile valley, Syria's plains, and Iraq's great irrigation works, and the caliphs invested in canals and land reclamation to raise revenue. Greek, Syriac, and Persian learning flowed into Arabic, beginning the translation tradition that would flower under the Abbasids. Controversies of the age still shape Islam: the legitimacy of dynastic rule versus merit, the status of converts, and above all Karbala, which fixed the Shia identity around loyalty to the Prophet's family and the sacred duty of mourning injustice. The Umayyads proved an empire could be built on Islam; their fall proved that an empire of Muslims had to do justice to all of them.

pageData.title: The Abbasid Caliphate
pageData.para1:
The Abbasid Caliphate. The revolution that swept the Umayyads away in 750 was raised in the name of the Prophet's family, promising a caliph from the house of Abbas, the Prophet's uncle. Its leader Abu al-Abbas was proclaimed in Kufa, the Umayyad armies were crushed on the Zab river, and the new dynasty moved the center of the Islamic world decisively eastward, from Mediterranean Syria to Iraq. In 762 the second caliph, al-Mansur, founded a new capital on the Tigris: Baghdad, the Round City, a perfect circle of walls and palaces at the meeting point of the trade routes of Iraq, Iran, Syria, and Egypt. It became within decades the largest and richest city on earth, perhaps half a million people, and the beating heart of a cosmopolitan empire. The early Abbasid century was the golden age of Islamic civilization.

Harun al-Rashid, caliph from 786 to 809, ruled at the height of its splendor, a figure whose court lives on in the tales of the Thousand and One Nights; his gifts to Charlemagne, including an elephant and a water clock that struck the hours, dazzled a Europe then far poorer. His son al-Ma'mun sponsored the great translation movement: at the House of Wisdom in Baghdad, scholars turned the Greek, Persian, and Indian classics into Arabic, then went beyond them. Al-Khwarizmi wrote the founding works of algebra, named for his book al-jabr, and of the decimal numerals the world now calls Arabic; al-Kindi, al-Farabi, and Ibn Sina, known in Latin as Avicenna, created philosophy and medicine studied in Europe for six centuries; astronomers measured the earth and refined the tables of the heavens; chemists, opticians, geographers, and historians worked in a common Arabic language of learning.

But the empire was already fracturing. Harun divided the succession between his sons, and the resulting civil war wrecked Baghdad from 809 to 813. Later caliphs came to rely on Turkish slave-soldiers, who soon made and murdered caliphs themselves; al-Mutawakkil's assassination in 861 opened a decade of anarchy. Spain was lost to the Umayyads, Egypt broke away under its own dynasties, and Iran fell to local Persian powers. In 945 the Buyids, Shia soldiers from Iran, took control of Baghdad and reduced the caliphs to figureheads, a condition that continued under the Sunni Seljuk Turks after 1055. The caliphate survived as a religious symbol until 1258, when the Mongol Hulagu sacked Baghdad, killed the caliph, and ended the classical Abbasid age. The revolution's organizers had learned from Umayyad failure, and the early Abbasids deliberately built a broader state.

They claimed legitimacy as the Prophet's kin, executed or pensioned off the revolutionary generals, and staffed the government with Persian secretaries whose families, like the Barmakids, ran the empire as viziers until their sudden fall. Al-Mansur, the dynasty's true founder, was an organizer of genius and suspicion: he built Baghdad, established the intelligence and postal service that reported the price of bread in every province, and crushed every rival, including the revolt of the Alids, the Prophet's descendants through Ali, whose failure pushed Shia hopes into patient waiting. The empire's wealth was stupendous: the geographers describe taxes from Egypt's grain, Iraq's Sawad, and the trade of the Gulf and the Indian Ocean flowing into Baghdad, whose palace ceremonial, the green dome, the curtain before the caliph, set the style of Islamic majesty.
